hypotheses.text: Motor development delay and sparse hair are the two most sensitive non-radiological phenotypic hallmarks of GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, each manifesting in greater than 90% of molecularly confirmed individuals across all aggregated cohorts.
hypotheses.rationale: Evaluating aggregated cohorts compiled across the literature allows testing whether motor delay and sparse hair serve as virtually obligate clinical indicators to triage patients before neuroimaging or exome sequencing.

evidence.text: In a comprehensive literature review of hitherto 28 patients with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, motor development delay was reported in 26 out of 28 individuals and sparse hair was documented in 26 out of 28 individuals.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: A large numbers of patients manifest motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), and speech disorder (24/28).

evidence.text: Salpietro et al. confirmed that individuals carrying bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in GTPBP1 or GTPBP2 consistently present with pathognomonic craniofacial features and ectodermal defects alongside profound neurodevelopmental impairment.

source.title: Bi-allelic genetic variants in the translational GTPases GTPBP1 and GTPBP2 cause a distinct identical neurodevelopmental syndrome
source.quote: Individuals with bi-allelic GTPBP1 or GTPBP2 variants presented with microcephaly, profound neurodevelopmental impairment, pathognomonic craniofacial features, and ectodermal defects.

hypotheses.text: Visual impairment and retinal dysfunction occur in less than 70% of reported GTPBP2 cases, precluding abnormal ophthalmologic examination from being an obligate criterion for diagnosis in early childhood.
hypotheses.rationale: While early literature (Jaberi et al., 2016) emphasized optic atrophy and photoreceptor/bipolar cell dysfunction as core features, broader cohort aggregations show that visual impairment is incomplete in penetrance or delayed in onset.

evidence.text: The aggregate literature review by Manoochehri et al. demonstrated that visual impairment was documented in only 18 out of 28 individuals with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, leaving over one-third of confirmed cases without reported visual deficits.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: Moreover, a significant fraction of patients suffer from intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28).

evidence.text: In the index family with a homozygous splice-site GTPBP2 mutation, full-field electroretinography showed generalized photoreceptor, bipolar, and amacrine cell dysfunction in all 3 affected siblings, suggesting visual deficits may be underreported due to lack of early specialized electroretinography.

source.title: Identification of mutation in GTPBP2 in patients of a family with neurodegeneration accompanied by iron deposition in the brain
source.quote: A full-field electroretinography revealed generalized dysfunction of photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and amacrine cells.

hypotheses.text: Skeletal anomalies (such as kyphoscoliosis or contractures) are present in approximately 80% of individuals with classic GTPBP2 truncating variants, but can be completely absent in patients with non-truncating missense variants.
hypotheses.rationale: Phenotype-genotype correlations remain unestablished; determining whether skeletal manifestations are tied to variant class or secondary to prolonged spasticity/hypotonia clarifies their role in early differential diagnosis.

evidence.text: Manoochehri et al. identified a 3-year-old girl homozygous for a novel missense variant (p.Leu430Pro) who presented without any skeletal abnormalities, contrasting with the 23 out of 28 individuals in the aggregated literature who demonstrated skeletal problems.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: In spite of previous patients, the proband in this study did not exhibit any skeletal abnormalities... skeletal problems (23/28)

evidence.text: OMIM entry #617988 classifies skeletal abnormalities including kyphoscoliosis and abnormal hand or foot posturing as additional variable features rather than obligate core manifestations.

hypotheses.text: Epilepsy and choreoathetosis occur in a substantial subpopulation of GTPBP2 patients and differentiate GTPBP2/GTPBP1 translational GTPase syndromes from uncomplicated hereditary spastic paraplegias.
hypotheses.rationale: Distinguishing pure upper motor neuron diseases from GTPBP2 syndrome requires identifying hyperkinetic movement disorders and seizure phenotypes that are not explained by corticospinal tract degeneration alone.

evidence.text: Salpietro et al. observed that choreoathetoid movements and refractory epilepsy form part of the core neurologic phenotype in individuals with bi-allelic GTPBP1 or GTPBP2 loss-of-function variants.

source.title: Bi-allelic genetic variants in the translational GTPases GTPBP1 and GTPBP2 cause a distinct identical neurodevelopmental syndrome
source.quote: Abnormal vision and/or hearing, progressive spasticity, choreoathetoid movements, refractory epilepsy, and brain atrophy were part of the core phenotype of this syndrome.

evidence.text: Vedula et al. reported a novel GTPBP2 variant causing syndromic epilepsy in Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, highlighting refractory seizures as a presenting and management-defining feature.

new_directions.question_text: What is the breakdown of seizure frequency, seizure semiology (e.g. focal vs. generalized tonic-clonic vs. infantile spasms), and EEG patterns across molecularly confirmed GTPBP2 cases?
new_directions.rationale: Epilepsy is highlighted as a core or defining feature in recent series (Vedula 2026, Salpietro 2024), but its exact penetrance across the ~28 documented patients has not been systematically compiled against age of onset.

new_directions.question_text: How do the facial dysmorphisms and ectodermal findings in GTPBP1-related disorder compare with GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome to determine if they are clinically indistinguishable without sequencing?
new_directions.rationale: Salpietro et al. (2024) asserted an identical syndrome caused by GTPBP1 and GTPBP2; determining if specific facial or ectodermal dysmorphologies distinguish them or if they form an inseparable clinical entity is essential for dysmorphology-based triage.
